citation.title: Deep learning aided topology optimization of phononic crystals
citation.authors: Paweł Kudela, Abdalraheem Ijjeh, Maciej Radzienski, Marco Miniaci, Nicola Pugno, Wieslaw Ostachowicz

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: A surrogate deep model predicts phononic crystal dispersion diagrams far faster than the conventional FEM solver, enabling its use within genetic-algorithm topology optimization.
claim.key_phrase: ultrafast in predicting the dispersion diagrams
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: The conclusion reports DL prediction in less than 100 ms and ordinary FEM calculation in approximately 0.5–1 h. Using the shorter FEM time and the upper bound of 0.1 s gives a conservative lower-bound ratio of 1,800 s / 0.1 s = 18,000; actual factor is greater.
claim.alternatives: Conclusion: DL predicts dispersion curves in under 100 ms versus approximately 0.5–1 h for FEM. Introduction: a 14,072-element, 134,040-DOF mesh took about 47 min to compute 24 eigenmodes.

baseline.classical_method: Finite element method (FEM) eigenvalue solution for phononic crystal dispersion curves
baseline.implementation: COMSOL Multiphysics; mesh generated with GMSH; COMSOL automated through MATLAB Live-Link (Sections 2.1–2.3)
baseline.hardware_classical: AMD Ryzen 7 1800X eight-core 3.8 GHz processor, 64 GB RAM (Section 2.1)
baseline.problem_size: 3D unit cell mesh with 14,072 tetrahedral elements and 134,040 degrees of freedom; 24 eigenmodes (Section 2.1); unit cell thickness 3 mm and width 8 mm (Section 2.2)
baseline.classical_iterations: not applicable; eigenmodes computed for dispersion diagram
baseline.classical_time: About 47 min for 24 eigenmodes in the stated mesh case (Section 2.1); ordinary FEM calculations approximately 0.5–1 h (Conclusion)
baseline.ml_time: Less than 100 ms per dispersion diagram prediction (Sections 2.1 and 4. Conclusions)
baseline.data_generation_cost: 9000 examples computed in COMSOL over about one month on a standard desktop computer (Section 2.3)
baseline.quality_metric: MSE and maximum frequency error against FEM dispersion diagrams; gap prediction (Sections 2.6, 3.2)
baseline.quality_gap: Testing MSE [kHz²]: 9.8 cross-like, 12.1 diagonal-like, 8.1 blot-like; maximum frequency errors in examples range 9.1–15.4 kHz (Section 2.6)

R1.evidence: Sections 2.6 and 3.2 compare DL predictions with FEM results and report error metrics, including FEM checks of optimized designs, but no equal-quality or equal-time optimization comparison is made; a selected F4 GA case has multiple bandgaps predicted incorrectly.

R2.evidence: Section 2.1 identifies COMSOL and a Ryzen CPU for FEM, but hardware for DL prediction is not reported, so the hardware comparison is not justified or matched.

R3.evidence: Section 2.3 reports roughly one month to generate 9,000 FEM examples, while training time and break-even uses are absent; the introduction notes the training-time cost but does not quantify it.

R4.evidence: Sections 2.6 and 3.2 check predicted dispersion diagrams against FEM, including selected optimized outputs, but do not report a failure or infeasibility rate; one selected F4 case has incorrect multiple-bandgap predictions.

reporting.n_test_cases: 300 testing examples (100 per each of three cavity types; Section 2.6); two illustrative GA runs are reported for each of three selected objective functions (Section 3.2)

notes: A dataset is linked via Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.8063241 (Section 2.3); no public code or code license is stated in the article.
